Discover What You Know
Learning Objectives
Review the anatomy of the hip, including the relevant musculature and neurovascular
structures.
Describe the four main approaches to the hip: direct anterior, anterolateral, direct lateral, and
posterolateral.
Identify the limitations and complications related to each surgical approach to the hip.
Overview
Acetabular Quadrant System
Acetabular anatomy is best understood using the acetabular quadrant system.
The quadrants are defined by a line drawn from the anterior superior iliac spine through the
center of the acetabulum. This line defines the anterior and posterior quadrants and is then

Osteology
Anatomy of the Pelvis and the Acetabulum
The pelvis is formed by two innominate bones that join in the midline at the sacrum. The
acetabulum of the hip is formed from three separate ossification centers: the ilium, ischium,
and pubis.1
The hip is a ball-and-socket joint. Stability is primarily conferred by the bony anatomy and
capture of the femoral head within the acetabulum; it is further augmented by the acetabular
labrum and the hip capsule.
Important bony pelvic landmarks include the anterior superior iliac spine and the anterior
inferior iliac spine.
In most patients, the acetabular surface is oriented approximately 45° caudally and 15°
anteriorly.
The posterior and superior surfaces of the acetabulum have thicker cartilage to allow for
weight bearing and ambulation.
The hemispheric depth of the acetabulum allows approximately 170° of coverage of the
femoral head. The coverage of the acetabulum is further augmented by the labrum, which
runs circumferentially around the acetabulum. At the most inferior component, the labrum
turns into the transverse acetabular ligament. The inferior acetabular surface consists of the
cotyloid fossa, and the transverse acetabular ligament forms the base of the cotyloid fossa.
For total hip arthroplasty (THA), the important surgical acetabular landmarks include:
The anterior and posterior acetabular walls
The base of the fovea (Figure 1)
The transverse acetabular ligament
The anterior and posterior brims of the acetabulum help determine the native acetabular
version and that of the acetabular implant.
The base of the fovea determines the medialization depth of the acetabulum. It is important
to locate the base of the cotyloid fossa in severely arthritic hips because this structure often
may be overgrown with large osteophytes that must be removed to find the base of the
fovea. Failure to remove these medial osteophytes during THA may result in a lateralized
acetabular implant.

The transverse acetabular ligament is very helpful in dysplastic hips because it may aid in
determining the inferior-most base of the acetabulum and may serve as an anatomic
landmark for reaming.
Figure 1 Intraoperative photograph shows the base of the fovea of the acetabulum (arrow).
(Reproduced from Nam D: Surgical anatomy of the hip, in Lieberman JR, ed: AAOS
Comprehensive Orthopaedic Review, ed 3. Rosemont, IL, American Academy of Orthopaedic
Surgeons; 2020, pp 417-428.)
The placement of trans-acetabular screws can augment fixation of the acetabular implant,
and several important anatomic relationships must be considered.
The acetabulum is divided into four quadrants, as described by Wasielewski et al.2 These
quadrants indicate zones safe for trans-acetabular screw placement to avoid injury to the
neurovascular structures (Figure 2).

Figure 2 Illustration shows the quadrant system at the anatomic hip center. The posterior-
inferior and posterior-superior quadrants are recommended for the transacetabular fixation

The most commonly damaged vessels are the common femoral artery and the external iliac
artery. Injury may be caused by sharp retractor placement with a knife or electrocautery and
by replacing acetabular screws that perforate a vessel.
The safest area for screw placement is the posterior-superior quadrant, followed by the
posterior-inferior quadrant. If screws are used in the anterior-inferior and anterior-superior
quadrants, the screws must be placed within the bone to avoid vascular injury (Figures 3, 4,
and 5; Table 1).

Anatomy of the Femur
The femur is the longest and strongest bone in the human body.
The femur is mostly cylindrical and is anteriorly and laterally bowed in its midportion.
The extent of femoral bowing is critical because patients with excessive bowing will have
difficult placement of long, straight stems.
The Dorr index is a ratio of the femoral canal diameter at the level of the lesser trochanter to
its diameter at a point 10 cm distal to the lesser trochanter.
In most patients, the proximal metaphyses and the neck of the femur are anteverted
approximately 15° in relation to the posterior aspect of the femoral condyles.
Excessive anteversion may make femoral stem placement difficult. Attention should be given
to adjusting femoral implant version independent of the native anatomy.
Hips with developmental dysplasia often have excessive femoral neck anteversion.
The anatomy of the femoral head-neck junction has a very important quantification of the
angle between the head and neck, which is, on average, approximately 125° to 127°.
The mean anteversion of the femoral neck in relation to the posterior aspect of the femoral
condyles is 14°.

In most hips, the center of the femoral head is at the level of the tip of the greater trochanter.
In patients who have coxa valga, the center of the femoral head is above the greater
trochanter; in patients who have coxa vara, the center of the femoral head is below the tip of
the greater trochanter.
Vascular Anatomy
Acetabular Quadrant System
The external iliac artery and vein are found in the anterior-superior quadrant. The obturator
vessels are found in the anterior-inferior quadrant.1
Neurovascular Structures Surrounding the Hip
Blood supply to the femoral head with age
The blood supply to the femoral head develops and changes with age.
From birth to approximately 4 years, the major blood supply comes from the medial and
lateral femoral circumflex arteries (from the profunda femoris artery), with major
contributions from the artery of the ligamentum teres.
From 4 years to adulthood, the posterosuperior and posteroinferior retinacular arteries
(from the medial circumflex artery) are the major blood supply, with minimal supply from the
lateral circumflex and ligamentum teres arteries.
In adulthood, the major blood supply is from the medial femoral circumflex and lateral
epiphyseal arteries.
Common femoral vessels
The common femoral artery arises from the external iliac artery as it passes under the
inguinal ligament.
The common femoral artery passes anterior and medial to the hip capsule.
The common femoral vein is a continuation of the external iliac vein.
The common femoral vessels are the most commonly reported extrapelvic vascular
structures that are injured during THA.
The most common mechanism of vascular injury is errant retractor placement anterior to the
acetabulum.
The profundus, or the deep femoral artery, arises from the lateral aspect of the common
femoral artery approximately 3.5 cm below the inguinal ligament.

The profundus femoral artery travels between the pectineus and adductor longus muscles.
The lateral circumflex artery arises from the lateral side of the proximal profundus femoris
artery (Figure 6). The lateral circumflex artery has ascending and descending branches. The
medial circumflex artery most commonly comes from the posteromedial profundus femoris
artery but also may come directly from the femoral artery. It traverses between the
pectineus and psoas muscles, and it appears at the upper border of the quadratus femoris.
The superior gluteal vessels are branches of the posterior division of the internal iliac artery.
These vessels are closest to the hip as they exit from the sciatic notch. Superior gluteal artery
injury can occur during the placement of screws in the region of the sciatic notch. Avoiding
damage to the superior gluteal vessels can be accomplished by palpating the sciatic notch.
The inferior gluteal vessels and internal vessels are branches of the anterior division of the
internal iliac artery. These vessels exit the pelvis between the piriformis and coccygeus
muscles. These vessels can be injured by screws in the posterior column that are at least 5
mm past the bony margin.
Figure 6 Intraoperative photograph of a hip obtained during a direct, anterior surgical approach
shows the lateral femoral circumflex artery traversing the deep dissection. (Courtesy of H. John
Cooper, MD, New York, NY.)

External iliac artery and vein

The external iliac artery is a branch of the common iliac artery after the common iliac
bifurcates at the level of the L5-S1 vertebral disk.
Injury to the external iliac artery and vein has been reported during hip replacement.
The external iliac artery and vein can be damaged by retractors placed too far over the
anterior-superior acetabular margin.
Injury to the external iliac vessels can be avoided by placing screws in the posterior-superior
quadrant.
Obturator vessels
The obturator nerve, artery, and vein most often traverse the quadrilateral surface of the
pelvis together.
The nerve is located most superior, and the vein is located most inferior.
Nerves
Acetabular Quadrant System
The external iliac artery and vein are found in the anterior-superior quadrant. The obturator
vessels are found in the anterior-inferior quadrant1 (Figure 7).
Figure 7 Illustration shows the acetabular zones for screw insertion. Line A is formed by
drawing a line from the anterior superior iliac spine (ASIS) to the center of the acetabular

Intrapelvic Nerves
Sciatic Nerve
The sciatic nerve has contributions from L4, L5, S1, S2, and S3.
It consists of the anterior tibial division and the posterior common peroneal division. The
sciatic nerve most commonly is a single nervous structure that lies anterior and medial to the
piriformis muscle after it exits from the sciatic notch. It exits below the piriformis muscle.
The common peroneal division sciatic nerve fibers are located more laterally in the sciatic
nerve.
In as many as 10% of patients, the sciatic nerve has two divisions, tibial and peroneal, that are
distinct as they come from the sciatic notch.
Sciatic and peroneal nerve palsies are the most common forms of nerve injury after THA. The
most common nerve injury is to the peroneal nerve fibers during surgical exposure, with an
incidence ranging from 0.5% to 2.0%.
A common peroneal nerve injury is differentiated from a sciatic nerve injury via
electromyography and nerve conduction velocity studies. In combination, these techniques
demonstrate abnormal fibrillation in the short head of the biceps, which receives innervation
from both branches of the common peroneal nerve.
Therefore, the short head of the biceps is the only muscle innervated by the peroneal division
of the sciatic nerve above the level of the fibular head.
The sciatic nerve is injured most commonly by posterior acetabular retractors.
Lengthening of the extremity and revision hip surgery are risk factors.
Patients with peroneal nerve palsy had a mean lengthening of the sciatic nerve of 2.7 cm,
whereas patients with complete sciatic nerve palsy had a mean lengthening of 4.4 cm.
Femoral Nerve
The femoral nerve is formed by branches from L2, L3, and L4. It lies on top of the iliopsoas
muscle and traverses into the leg through the femoral triangle.

The femoral triangle is anterior and medial to the hip joint; it is in this area that the nerve is
susceptible to injury.
The femoral triangle has specific borders and is defined by the inguinal ligament proximally,
the sartorius muscle laterally, and the adductor longus medially. The floor or dorsal aspect of
the triangle is made up of the iliopsoas and pectineus muscles, and the roof or ventral aspect
is made up of the overlying fascia.
The femoral artery, nerve, and vein traverse this area. Moving from lateral to medial, the
structures are nerve, artery, and vein.
The femoral nerve supplies innervation to the iliacus, pectineus, sartorius, and quadriceps
muscles.
The incidence of femoral nerve palsy is approximately 2.3%.
The most common mechanism of femoral nerve injury is retractor placement.
Lateral Femoral Cutaneous Nerve
The lateral femoral cutaneous nerve arises from the L2 and L3 nerve roots. It comes from the
psoas muscle at its lateral border.
The most common mechanism of injury during THA is the use of the Smith Petersen or
anterior approach.
Obturator Nerve
The obturator nerve comes from nerve roots L2, L3, and L4.
Obturator nerve injury is an extremely rare complication of THA. It can manifest as persistent
groin pain after THA.
Joints and Ligaments
Hip Capsule and Ligaments
The hip capsule attaches anteriorly and posteriorly along the periphery of the acetabulum
outside the labrum. Inferiorly, the hip capsule is attached to the acetabular labrum1 (Figure 8).
The capsule is attached to the femur anteriorly along the intertrochanteric crest. On the
posterior side, it attaches only partially, therefore, the basicervical region of the femoral neck
and the intertrochanteric region of the femur are not intracapsular.

The iliofemoral and pubofemoral ligaments reinforce the anterior hip capsule, whereas the
ischiofemoral ligament reinforces the posterior capsule.
The iliofemoral ligament also is known as the Y ligament of Bigelow; it originates at the
anterior inferior iliac spine and inserts at the intertrochanteric line.
The iliofemoral ligament becomes taut in full extension, preventing anterior dislocation and
hyperextension of the hip. This structure may become very contracted in patients with severe
hip arthritis and may require release intraoperatively to relieve an internal and flexion
contracture of the hip.
The pubofemoral ligament attaches to the inferior and medial part of the capsule. It may cause
a hip adduction contracture.
The ischiofemoral ligament reinforces the posterior capsule; it provides a check to internal
rotation of the hip.
The twisted orientation of the hip ligaments provides a screw mechanism for the hip in full
extension.
The ligamentum teres originates in the cotyloid fossa and attaches on the fovea of the femoral
head.
The sacrospinous and sacrotuberous ligaments create the boundaries of the greater and
lesser sciatic foramina.
The sacrospinous ligament creates the upper border of the lesser sciatic foramen and the
lower border of the greater sciatic foramen.
The sacrotuberous ligament creates the inferior border of the lesser sciatic foramen.
The piriformis muscle and the sciatic nerve exit from the greater sciatic foramen.
The short external rotator muscles exit from the lesser sciatic foramen.

The mean range of motion of a normal hip that is unaffected by arthritis is approximately
120° of flexion, 30° of extension, 45° of abduction, 20° to 30° of adduction, 35° of internal
rotation, and 45° of external rotation.
Normal gait function requires 30° of hip flexion, 10° of hyperextension, 5° of abduction and
adduction, and 5° of internal and external rotation.
Hip flexor muscles (Tables 2, 3, and 4)
The primary hip flexor muscles are the iliopsoas, rectus femoris, and sartorius muscles. The
tensor fascia latae (TFL) is a secondary hip flexor.
The iliopsoas muscle has a large origin along the iliac crest, iliac fossa, sacra ala, iliolumbar
ligaments, and sacroiliac ligaments. This large muscle also has origins along the bodies of the
T12 through L4 thoracic lumbar vertebra, transverse process of the first through fifth lumbar
vertebra, and intervertebral disks.
The rectus femoris crosses the hip joint and the knee joint. The straight head originates from
the anterior inferior iliac spine, whereas the reflected head originates from the supra-
acetabular tubercle at the superior-anterior edge of the acetabulum. The rectus femoris
flexes the hip joint and extends the knee joint. Simultaneous hip flexion and knee extension
considerably shorten the muscle across both joints.
The sartorius muscle originates on the anterior superior iliac spine, crosses the hip and knee
joints, and inserts on the medial aspect of the tibia and the pes anserine complex.

The TFL muscle originates laterally on the anterolateral edge of the iliac crest. Its muscle
fibers combine with the fasciae latae to form the iliotibial band. The action of the TFL is to
flex, abduct, and rotate the hip (Figure 9).
Other flexors of the hip muscle include the pectineus, adductor longus, adductor brevis,
magnus, and gracilis muscles.
Figure 9 Intraoperative photograph of a hip obtained during a direct, anterior surgical
approach shows the tensor fasciae latae during superficial dissection. (Courtesy of H. John
Cooper, MD, New York, NY.)
Hip extensor muscles
The gluteus maximus and hamstring muscles are the most important hip joint extensors.
The gluteus maximus originates from the sacrum, the coccyx, and the sacrotuberous
ligaments. It inserts into the lateral intramuscular septum on the femur. During hip surgery,
excessive internal rotation of the hip for prolonged periods may cause injury to the sciatic
nerve under the gluteus maximus tendon. This phenomenon may result in sciatic nerve
palsy.
The hamstring muscles originate on the ischial tuberosity. The medial hamstring inserts on
the medial tibia, whereas the biceps femoris inserts on the fibular head.
Hip abductor muscles
The predominant abductors of the hip are the gluteus medius and gluteus minimus muscles.

The gluteus medius has three different components: anterior, middle, and posterior (Figure
10).
The gluteus medius and minimus muscles function together to maintain and abduct the
femur during the stance phase of gait.
A Trendelenburg lurch is an attempt by the body to compensate for abductor weakness by
bringing the center of gravity closer to the hip center, forcing the patient to lean toward the
affected side.
Damage and/or weakness to the abductor muscles may occur during surgical approaches to
the hip. These injuries may affect the abductor muscles or the nerve supply to the muscles. If
major damage to the abductor muscles occurs, hip stability can be affected, and repair or
reconstruction of the abductors or the use of more constrained hip implants may be
considered.

External rotator muscles

The external rotators of the hip include the obturator internus and externus, superior and
inferior gemelli, quadratus femoris, and piriformis muscles.
The obturator internus muscle originates from the inner component of the obturator
foramen and emerges through the lesser sciatic foramen.
The gemelli muscles have an approximate location to the obturator internus.
The piriformis muscle originates from the greater sciatic foramen and inserts onto the
greater trochanter.
The piriformis forms the reference structure for the posterior part of the hip. Structures are
identified by whether they originate above or below the piriformis.
The superior gluteal nerve and artery exit the pelvis above the piriformis muscle, whereas
the pudendal nerve, the internal pudendal artery, the nerve to the obturator internus, the
posterior femoral cutaneous nerve, the sciatic nerve, the inferior gluteal nerve, the inferior
gluteal artery, and the nerve to the quadratus femoris exit the pelvis below the piriformis
muscle.
In 10% of patients, the common peroneal component of the sciatic nerve can pass through
the division in the piriformis.
Most often, the sciatic nerve passes below the piriformis and is situated on top of the short
external rotators.
The best method to protect the sciatic nerve during a posterior approach is to maintain
retractors within the posterior hip capsule, thereby protecting the nerve.
Internal rotator muscles
Internal rotation of the hip is performed by muscles that have primary functions other than
internal rotation. Therefore, internal rotation is a secondary function of those muscle groups.
The most consistent internal rotators of the hip joint are the gluteus medius and TFL
muscles.

Direct Anterior Approach
Background
Commonly referred to as the Smith-Petersen approach3
First described in 1881
Technique
Patient is placed in the supine position on a traction table or a standard orthopaedic table.

The incision starts 1 cm distal and 3 cm lateral to the tip of the anterior superior iliac spine
and extends distally 8 to 10 cm toward the lateral border of the patella over the TFL muscle
belly. The skin is incised, and deep dissection is carried out to the fascia overlying the TFL.
The fascia is sharply incised in line with the incision, over the TFL muscle belly. The medial
flap of the fascia is elevated, and the TFL muscle is released from its undersurface and
retracted laterally.
The internervous plane between the sartorius muscle (femoral nerve) and the TFL (superior
gluteal nerve) superficially and between the rectus femoris (femoral nerve) and the gluteus
medius (superior gluteal nerve) deep are then opened, exposing the hip capsule. The
ascending branch of the lateral circumflex vessels must be identified and coagulated deep to
the TFL (Figure 11).

Anterolateral Approach
Background
Commonly known as the Watson-Jones approach
Interval
The patient is placed in the lateral decubitus position or the supine position with the surgical
extremity draped free (Videos 4 and 5).
The incision is positioned over the lateral aspect of the hip, starting 2 to 3 cm proximal to the
anterosuperior aspect of the greater trochanter and extending distally in line with the femur.
The skin and subcutaneous tissue are incised to the fascia. The fascia is incised posterior to
the TFL. The gluteus medius and the vastus lateralis are exposed.5 (Resource 3)
The classic anterolateral approach involves detachment of the anterior one-third of the
gluteus medius from the greater trochanter with or without a bone fragment. Modifications
of this approach often are performed without detachment of the gluteus medius.
The intermuscular interval used is posterior to the TFL and anterior to the gluteus medius.5
The anterior aspect of the gluteus minimus muscle is released from its insertion, allowing for
exposure of the anterior hip capsule.

Advantages
Most commonly used approach worldwide; familiar to many surgeons throughout their
training
Spares the hip abductors; therefore, associated with a lower risk of postoperative abductor
insufficiency5
Associated with a lower risk of heterotopic bone formation, intraoperative femur fracture,
lateral femoral cutaneous nerve neuropraxia, and superior gluteal nerve palsy5
Is extensile, allowing access to the femur and the ilium/pelvis, if necessary, during complex
procedures. Because of its wide exposure, it is used in primary and revision THA, hip
resurfacing, fixation of acetabular fractures, and drainage of septic hips.9 (Resource 5)
Limitations and complications
Historically, a higher dislocation rate; repair of the posterior capsule and the short external
rotators has improved the dislocation rate to a rate comparable with those of other
approaches.10 (Resource 6)
Highest incidence of injury to the sciatic nerve;5 the peroneal branch is most often affected.
The femoral nerve is at risk for injury with anterior acetabular retractor placement.9
